name: The Test Scout
oneLiner: Collapses a feature's scattered artifacts — ADO work items, design docs, meeting transcripts — into one structured, testable briefing.
lead: Kills the per-story ramp-up where a tester reconstructs a feature from ADO, Figma, specs, and a meeting recording. One command aggregates all of it into a structured briefing — flows, business rules, edge cases, integration points, open questions, confidence score — so the whole team tests against one model instead of re-deriving it story by story.
chore: A tester picks up a story with a three-line description. The real detail is spread across a Figma deck, a spec doc, an hour of recording, and child work items. Reconstructing a testable model by hand is slow and brittle — one missed decision silently changes the expected behavior.
instead: Point it at a story ID and a document folder. It walks the ADO work-item tree, extracts text (pdf-parse for PDFs, mammoth for Word, a VTT parser for transcripts), sends transcripts to Gemini Flash for demonstrated behavior and decisions, then merges everything into a content-hashed JSON briefing: purpose, flows, business rules, edge cases, integration points, open questions, and a 0–100 confidence score. Re-runs are incremental — only changed sources are re-parsed.
whyItMatters: A misunderstood feature produces the wrong test cases, and the defect ships however green they are. Shared understanding up front is the highest-leverage point in the QA cycle.

howItWorks.step: Pulls the feature's ticket and its smaller child tickets from the team's shared work board, keeping the ones about how the feature looks and behaves and skipping the plumbing.
howItWorks.explain: Pure keyword routing, no LLM — the same ticket always lands in the same bucket, which keeps the briefing's scope auditable. It concatenates `title` and `description` and lowercases once into `combined`, then checks `IGNORE_KEYWORDS` **first**: order is deliberate — a plumbing ticket that also says 'form' must be dropped before the UI check can claim it, so the ignore pass short-circuits with `return 'ignore'`. Only then does it scan `uiKeywords`, then `funcKeywords`, returning on the first hit, so **first match wins**. The final `return 'other'` is a keep, not a skip — an unmatched ticket still lands in the briefing, just uncategorized, so nothing silently disappears.

howItWorks.step: Opens the supporting files in the feature folder — design mock-ups (PDF), written specs (Word), and recorded meeting transcripts.
howItWorks.explain: Aggregates every artifact into one flat `sources` array where each entry carries a `type` tag, so downstream extraction can treat a PDF, a story export, and a transcript uniformly. It seeds the array with `loadLocalAdoStories(config.adoDir)` first, then probes a fixed list of conventional design-folder names — `design`, `figma`, `designs`, `wireframes` — because teams don't agree on one name; the `fs.existsSync(dir)` guard means a missing folder is silently skipped rather than throwing. Each loaded design doc is tagged `'design'` so a later stage knows how to parse it. Transcripts are deliberately **not** loaded here — they need LLM analysis rather than plain extraction, so they're handled in a separate pass.

howItWorks.step: Feeds the meeting transcripts to an AI reader that pulls out the demonstrated behaviour, the decisions made, and the open questions.
howItWorks.explain: The transcript is the one source the rule-based extractors can't handle, so it's the only place an LLM is used here. The prompt pins the model to a QA-analyst role and hard-caps its inputs — `featureContext.substring(0, 2000)` and `transcript.substring(0, 6000)` — a deliberate token-budget guard so an hour-long recording can't overflow the context window or spike cost; the head of each carries the demoed behavior. It demands a fixed JSON shape (`demonstratedFeatures`, `testableScenarios`, `businessRules`, `edgeCases` with a `priority` enum) so the output slots straight into the briefing. `parseLLMJson` rather than `JSON.parse` because models routinely wrap JSON in markdown fences or prose — the tolerant parser salvages the object instead of throwing.

howItWorks.step: Merges everything into one structured briefing — purpose, user flows, rules, edge cases, integration points — and gives it a confidence score.
howItWorks.explain: Two extraction strategies converge into one object. The four `extract*` calls are pure rule-based passes over **every** source, so UI components, flows, rules, and edge cases are recovered deterministically without a model. The transcript-only loop then mines `walkthrough` data the rules can't infer: it regex-slices the `## Decisions Made` markdown section out of each transcript's content — the lookahead `(?=\n##|$)` stops the capture at the next heading or end-of-string so it grabs exactly that section — and `parseList` turns the bullet block into entries. Finally `score(sources)` weights how many source types were present into the `confidenceScore`, so a briefing built from three artifacts is marked more trustworthy than one from a single thin ticket.

howItWorks.step: Saves the briefing so the next agent in the line (the Test-Plan Author) can build test cases straight from it.
howItWorks.explain: The briefing is the hand-off artifact, so persistence is deliberately plain and durable. `getVersionFilePath` derives a stable per-story path so re-runs overwrite the same file rather than piling up copies. `fs.mkdirSync(..., { recursive: true })` creates the whole output directory tree in one call and is a no-op if it already exists, so the first run on a fresh checkout doesn't fail on a missing folder. It writes `JSON.stringify(version, null, 2)` — pretty-printed at 2-space — so the file stays diff-friendly and human-readable, and because `version` already carries the content hashes, the next run can tell what actually changed.

examples.caption: A new 'save draft' feature with thin paperwork
examples.input: A feature ticket that just says 'Users can save a draft', plus a folder holding two screen mock-ups and a 40-minute recorded design meeting.
examples.output: A briefing that spells out the flow (click Save Draft, see a 'Draft saved' banner, drafts appear under a Drafts tab), the rule (drafts expire after 30 days), an edge case (saving with an empty title should be blocked), and one open question the meeting never resolved: 'What happens to a draft if the user logs out?'

examples.caption: A messy meeting transcript
examples.input: An hour-long walkthrough recording where the team argued about button placement and settled on a final design.
examples.output: A short list of decisions ('Continue button moved to bottom-right', 'error banner is red, not amber'), the testable scenarios that were demonstrated, and the follow-up questions nobody answered.

underHood.heading: Reads the shared work board
underHood.whenRuns: First, the moment the agent starts on a feature.
underHood.output: The parent story plus its child tickets, filtered down to the ones about behaviour and screens (via the Azure DevOps REST API — the team's shared work-and-ticket board).

underHood.heading: Parses the local documents
underHood.whenRuns: Right after the tickets are pulled.
underHood.input: The PDFs, Word docs, and meeting-transcript files sitting in the feature folder.
underHood.output: Plain, searchable text — using pdf-parse for PDFs, mammoth for Word, and VTT/DOCX parsers for transcripts.

underHood.heading: Summarizes transcripts with an AI model
underHood.whenRuns: Once for each recorded meeting it finds.
underHood.input: The transcript text and a short summary of the feature.
underHood.output: A structured list of demonstrated features, decisions made, and open questions (produced by the Gemini Flash model).

underHood.heading: Merges into one 'intelligence' file
underHood.whenRuns: After every source has been read.
underHood.output: A single structured JSON briefing, stamped with content hashes for change-tracking and a 0–100 confidence score.

underHood.heading: Understanding first, test cases later
underHood.whenRuns: Only if you explicitly ask for it.
underHood.output: By default the agent stops at understanding; it will not write test cases unless told to — so it is safe to run just to learn a feature.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Read access to your Azure DevOps project and a personal access token (Work Items: Read).
A folder for the feature with its documents — design PDFs, spec `.docx` files, and any meeting-transcript (`.vtt`/`.docx`) files.
A Gemini API key for the transcript-summarization step; without it the agent still runs, rule-based only.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the engine that runs the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a small TypeScript program; Node is the runtime that executes it. This is the one thing you install once per machine.
steps.firstRun: Needed only the first time on a new computer.

steps.label: Get the agent's code and install the libraries it depends on.
steps.why: `npm install` downloads the helper libraries the agent uses — the work-board client, the PDF reader, the Word reader, and the AI client — into a local `node_modules` folder.
steps.rerun: Skips straight past — already installed, unless the library list changed.

steps.label: Tell it which systems to talk to (environment variables).
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORG=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-gemini-key   # optional
steps.why: The agent reads these at startup to know which work board to open, which token proves it's allowed, and which AI to use. Nothing is hard-coded — swap these and it points at a different project.

steps.label: Point it at one feature and run it.
steps.why: This is the actual run. `npm run intelligence:folder` launches the agent's built-in "read a feature folder" task — one of the named shortcuts defined in its `package.json` (think of it as pressing a labelled button that runs the real program underneath). The lone `--` is npm's way of saying "everything after this belongs to the agent, not to npm", so the two options are passed straight through: `--story` is the feature's ticket number and `--folder` is where its documents live. Hitting Enter starts the whole read-and-summarize.
steps.firstRun: Reads every source from scratch and builds the briefing.
steps.rerun: Only re-reads the documents that actually changed (it fingerprints each one), then writes a short changelog of what's different.

steps.label: Open the briefing it produced.
steps.cmd:
open ./output/intelligence/story-4001.json
# and the readable summary:
open ./output/intelligence/story-4001.md
steps.why: The agent saves its work to disk. The `.json` is the structured briefing (for the next agent to consume); the `.md` is the same thing formatted for a human to read.

inputs.name: --story <id>
inputs.desc: The feature's ticket number on the work board.

inputs.name: --folder <path>
inputs.desc: A folder holding the feature's design PDFs, spec Word docs, and meeting transcripts.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: Which board/project to read, the access token, and (optionally) the AI key.

outputs.name: story-<id>.json
outputs.desc: The structured briefing — purpose, user flows, rules, edge cases, open questions, and a confidence score.

outputs.name: story-<id>.md
outputs.desc: The same briefing formatted for a person to read.

outputs.name: changelog (on re-run)
outputs.desc: A short list of what changed since last time, so you don't re-read the whole thing.

runbook.rerun: The second run is fast and quiet: the agent stored a fingerprint of every document it read, so it only re-summarizes the ones that actually changed and prints a changelog. Run it on a schedule and the briefing stays current on its own.
runbook.integrate: The `.json` output is the hand-off to the next agent in the line — the **Test-Plan Author** — which turns the briefing straight into test cases. Drop this step into your CI pipeline so every new feature ticket automatically gets a briefing waiting for the tester.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: point the agent at a feature and watch the briefing appear.
script: Open a terminal beside the feature folder so viewers see both.
Say: 'This agent reads everything about a feature and hands back one briefing. Watch.'
Show the feature folder — point out the design PDF, the spec doc, the meeting transcript.
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; say one line about what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's already done); explain it's grabbing the helper libraries.
Show the three `export` lines; say 'this is the only place the client-specific stuff lives.'
Run the `npm run intelligence:folder -- --story 4001 --folder ...` command; narrate the log lines as it reads each source.
Open the produced `.md` briefing; read out the flows, rules, and the one open question it surfaced.
Re-run the same command; show it's near-instant and prints a changelog. Say 'that's the fingerprinting — it only re-reads what changed.'
Close: 'The .json it wrote is what the next agent turns into test cases.'

outputSample.heading: Its output can become an HTML page — via any LLM
outputSample.whenRuns: An optional step after the briefing is saved.
outputSample.input: The `.json` briefing (for the next agent to consume) or the human-readable `.md`.
outputSample.output: Because the briefing is plain, structured text, you can hand it to any LLM and ask for a polished HTML page, a slide, or a one-pager — no special integration needed. The sample beside this was generated straight from `story-4001.json`.
outputSample.imgAlt: A sample HTML briefing page generated from the agent's JSON output
outputSample.caption: Sample: the briefing turned into an HTML page by an LLM.
